sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: AI coworkers must coordinate tools, communicate across turns, and act on changing workspace state while respecting workflow constraints. Constructing training experience for these capabilities requires coherent requests, service records, tool interfaces, and grading checks. We present CoworkEnv, a capability-guided framework for synthesizing executable training environments for AI coworkers. Workflow requirements guide task construction, and programmatic validation with feedback repair checks generated specifications and grading behavior. Teacher executions yield curated demonstrations for supervised fine-tuning (SFT), while student interactions provide rollouts and rewards for reinforcement learning (RL). Using these resources, we train compact PocketWorker models. For Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct, SFT raises the mean score from 46.6 to 64.1 on Claw-Eval, including a 31.9-point gain on Multi-turn tasks. An SFT-only extension to ClawMark demonstrates applicability across coworker benchmarks. We further compare RL training dynamics across configurations that vary reward processing and credit assignment. Improving training rewards provide preliminary evidence that the constructed environments support policy optimization.

Constructing training experience for these capabilities requires coherent requests, service records, tool interfaces, and grading checks. We present CoworkEnv, capability-guided framework for synthesizing executable training environments for AI coworkers. Workflow requirements guide task construction, and programmatic validation with feedback repair checks generated specifications and grading behavior. Teacher executions yield curated demonstrations for supervised fine-tuning (SFT), while student interactions provide rollouts and rewards for reinforcement learning (RL). Using these resources, we train compact PocketWorker models. For Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct, SFT raises the mean score from 46.6 to 64.1 on Claw-Eval, including 31.9-point gain on Multi-turn tasks. An SFT-only extension to ClawMark demonstrates applicability across coworker benchmarks. We further compare RL training dynamics across configurations that vary reward processing and credit assignment. Improving training rewards provide preliminary evidence that the constructed environments support policy optimization. 1. Introduction AI coworkers are expected to carry out everyday work through sustained interaction with users, tools, and changing workspace. Resolving customer-support request, for example, can require consulting account history, locating relevant procedure, and updating the correct ticket while respecting access restrictions. Such workflows combine multi-turn communication, information gathering, tool coordination, and decisions about when to act [Trivedi et al., 2024, Xu et al., 2026b, Yao et al., 2024]. Recent coworker models and benchmarks make these capabilities explicit targets for agent development [Chen et al., 2026a, Meng et al., 2026, Wang et al., 2026b, Ye et al., 2026]. Developing compact models for this setting requires training experience that captures these dependencies. Constructing that experience is central challenge. The information needed to complete workflow is often distributed across documents, service records, and intermediate environment state. Synthesizing useful task therefore requires the request, the available evidence, and the permitted actions to fit together. Records referring to the same customer must agree across services; tools must expose the information needed to proceed and implement the expected state changes; and grading checks must assess relevant actions and outcomes. plausible final response alone cannot establish that the intended update occurred or that prohibited action was avoided. These requirements make executable environment construction and verification integral to data synthesis, as also emphasized in coworker evaluation and computer-use training [Meng et al., 2026, Wang et al., 2026a]. CoworkEnv: Synthesizing Training Environments for Long-Horizon Cowork Agents Open agent-training efforts have begun to expose the data choices behind capable systems. NemotronTerminal and SERA study synthetic tasks and demonstrations for terminal and coding agents, while OpenThoughts-Agent investigates data curation across agentic tasks [Pi et al., 2026, Raoof et al., 2026, Shen et al., 2026]. Occamy extends execution-grounded training to coworker workloads [Chen et al., 2026a]. Building on these efforts, we focus on practical question: how can targeted coworker capabilities be translated into executable training tasks that support both imitation and learning from interaction? We present CoworkEnv, capability-guided framework for synthesizing executable training environments for AI coworkers. Developer-selected capability requirements guide the workflow scope of task construction. workflow specification is implemented as request, initial service records, tool interfaces, and grading checks. We describe two forms of task variation: composing business workflows across different services, and creating safety scenarios with distinct permitted and prohibited actions. Resolving customer-support issue, for example, connects CRM context with helpdesk ticket and knowledge-base procedure; investigating payment-change request connects correspondence with financial history. In the documented safety-task family, generation agents draft task content and separate grading role defines the execution checks. Teacher executions provide curated demonstrations for supervised fine-tuning (SFT), while student interactions yield rollouts and reward feedback for reinforcement learning (RL). This process separates the construction of problem from the generation of attempts to solve it. Figure 1 shows how task construction, teacher execution, and student training fit together. To assess the training utility of these resources, we fine-tune Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct [Bai et al., 2025] to obtain PocketWorker-8B. SFT raises the mean score from 46.6 to 64.1 on Claw-Eval tasks, with 31.9-point gain on Multi-turn tasks. separate SFT-only application to ClawMark extends the evaluation to second coworker benchmark. We also compare training configurations for GRPO, Dr.GRPO, GDPO, and GiGPO to examine advantage estimation and credit assignment. Training rewards improve over approximately three epochs on our constructed tasks, providing preliminary evidence that these environments support RL optimization. Our contributions are: ① Capability-guided synthesis of executable coworker environments. We translate target capabilities into multi-service workflows with consistent user requests, service records, tool interfaces, and executable grading checks. Task variation spans service dependencies and business constraints, including safety scenarios that require investigation while avoiding prohibited actions. Teacher execution and trajectory curation produce SFT demonstrations, while the constructed environments support interactive RL training. ② Training utility and analysis. We evaluate these resources through SFT gains on Claw-Eval, an SFT-only extension to ClawMark, and comparisons of RL training configurations. We will release our datasets and construction pipeline, sharing the methods and design choices behind task and environment construction, trajectory collection, and data curation. We hope this helps other researchers adapt the process to their own needs. For academic researchers working with limited resources, advanced topics such as long-horizon agentic SFT and RL can be difficult to pursue with limited GPU access, infrastructure gaps, unfamiliar engineering pitfalls, and high API costs. Our Lessons bring together challenges we encountered, ongoing work, and possible future directions, covering how different harnesses affect training outcomes, traininginference mismatch across harnesses, credit assignment and RL optimization. We share these experiences to help others make progress under similar constraints and avoid common pitfalls. CoworkEnv: Synthesizing Training Environments for Long-Horizon Cowork Agents 2. Related Work Agent post-training. Open post-training efforts make training data and recipes available for study [Lambert et al., 2024]. AgentTuning develops general agent abilities through instruction tuning, while Nemotron-Terminal, OpenThoughts-Agent, and SERA investigate task generation and trajectory curation for terminal, coding, and broader agentic behavior [Pi et al., 2026, Raoof et al., 2026, Shen et al., 2026, Zeng et al., 2024]. Related recipes extend trajectory-based training to research, data analysis, and GUI workflows [Ding et al., 2026, Fang et al., 2025, Qiao et al., 2026]. AgentGym-RL and RAGEN study learning through sequential interaction, while ToolRL examines reward design for tool use [Qian et al., 2026, Wang et al., 2025, Xi et al., 2025]. slime provides post-training framework with customizable data generation for RL scaling [Zhu et al., 2025]. Agent harnesses organize execution and interaction interfaces [Huang et al., 2026, Xie et al., 2026b], with LEGORL connecting native coding-agent harnesses to policy-gradient training [Du et al., 2026]. Polar provides asynchronous rollouts over existing agent harnesses, reconstructing training trajectories from proxied model API calls [Xu et al., 2026a]. Building on PPO and GRPO [Schulman et al., 2017, Shao et al., 2024], subsequent methods explore advantage and loss normalization, reward-component normalization, and finer-grained credit assignment [Feng et al., 2025, Liu et al., 2026a, 2025c, Wei et al., 2025]. Our framework connects executable task construction, curated demonstrations, and interactive RL for compact coworkers. Executable task synthesis and demonstration curation. Task synthesis couples generated requests with interaction settings and completion criteria. AgentGen and MATRIX construct environments or simulated scenarios [Hu et al., 2025, Tang et al., 2025]; APIGen-MT links task blueprints to multi-turn interactions, and CUA-Gym jointly constructs instructions, environments, and rewards [Prabhakar et al., 2026, Wang et al., 2026a]. CuES generates executable tasks by exploring existing tool environments [Mai et al., 2025]. Verification and refinement further shape training data: ToolACE verifies generated tool-use dialogues, while AgentRefine studies refinement-oriented demonstrations [Fu et al., 2025, Liu et al., 2025b]. Complementary approaches obtain training experience through environment models and adaptive generation: DreamGym and Qwen-AgentWorld simulate environment dynamics, PatchWorld induces executable world-model programs with counterexample-driven repair, and AgentEvolver combines task generation with experience-guided exploration [Bai et al., 2026, Chen et al., 2026b, Zhai et al., 2025, Zuo et al., 2026]. Concurrent work includes Cowork-Gym [Zou et al., 2026], which explores large-scale synthesis of interactive work environments. Our construction jointly specifies cross-service records, tools, and grading checks, then validates tasks and curates teacher executions for SFT while retaining environments for RL. Coworker agents and evaluation. Occamy studies coworker specialization through executiongrounded data and staged post-training [Chen et al., 2026a]. AppWorld, 𝜏-bench, TheAgentCompany, and AutomationBench evaluate multi-application work, user interaction, and workflow constraints [Shepard and Salimans, 2026, Trivedi et al., 2024, Xu et al., 2026b, Yao et al., 2024], while GDPval evaluates economically valuable professional tasks [Patwardhan et al., 2026]. ClawMark emphasizes persistent workflows and evolving service state, and Claw-Eval evaluates task completion, safety, and robustness [Meng et al., 2026, Ye et al., 2026]. AgentDojo and ToolEmu assess risks from prompt injection and agent actions [Debenedetti et al., 2024, Ruan et al., 2024]; Terminal-Bench and CyberGym provide execution-based evaluation in terminal and software-security settings [Merrill et al., 2026, Wang et al., 2026c]. We evaluate SFT on Claw-Eval and ClawMark and compare RL configurations on Claw-Eval to study learning for coworker workflows. CoworkEnv: Synthesizing Training Environments for Long-Horizon Cowork Agents 3. Method CoworkEnv constructs executable coworker environments through the following stages: capabilityguided task design, executable environment construction, programmatic validation and feedback repair, teacher execution and curation, and preparation for SFT or RL. The central unit is task environment that brings together request, the information and tools needed to act, and checks of the resulting execution. Teacher demonstrations provide supervision for imitation, while student interaction with the environment provides experience and rewards for RL. 3.1. Capability-Guided Task Synthesis From capabilities to task specifications. We translate target capabilities into coverage plan specifying service combinations, intended difficulty, and business scenarios. Scenarios define selection conditions, distractor records, and permitted actions; fixed reference date anchors time-sensitive requirements. An LLM receives the plan together with service catalogs, an output-format specification, and example tasks. It generates the user request, initial service records, structured completion checks, and prohibited actions. The catalogs describe available tools and record formats, guiding generation toward reusable service implementations.

sections.title: Limitations
sections.content: Execution scores measure the properties encoded by the graders. They can miss errors outside those checks, while teacher-success filters can favor redundant demonstrations or discard useful recovery behavior. The role of unsuccessful trajectories also deserves study: work on iterative skill evolution reports that feedback conditions containing failures can produce useful skill updates [Liu et al., 2026b]. Regenerating the original teacher trajectories may require access to proprietary model service.

sections.title: Ethical Considerations
sections.content: CoworkEnv is designed for research in executable, simulated work environments rather than deployment in real-world organizations. Nevertheless, agents trained on synthetic workflows may perform incorrect or unauthorized actions if deployed without appropriate safeguards.

Figure 3 compares training dynamics for GRPO, Dr.GRPO, GDPO, and GiGPO on our constructed task set. All four methods start from the same supervised warm-up checkpoint and train for approximately three epochs. Table 3 reports the final benchmark results for all four methods. The method-specific choices are described below. The GRPO baseline [Shao et al., 2024] centers the scalar reward within each group of eight rollouts and normalizes by the group standard deviation with denominator floor of 0.05. Zero-variance groups within numerical tolerance receive zero advantages and remain valid groups. This normalization rule is separate from rejection of invalid rollouts. Dr.GRPO. Following Liu et al. [2025c], our implementation changes both advantage normalization and loss normalization. Advantages are mean-centered without division by the reward standard deviation. The masked token losses are summed and divided by fixed normalizer of 1,536, corresponding to the per-turn generation limit of 1,536 tokens. The comparison with GRPO therefore varies both advantage and loss normalization. GDPO. Our GDPO implementation normalizes each reward dimension within the rollout group, combines the resulting advantages, and applies batch-wise normalization [Liu et al., 2026a]. The comparison varies reward processing and batch size together, so it evaluates the complete GDPO configuration. GiGPO. GiGPO combines episode-level advantages with step-level advantages computed from groups of matching intermediate states [Feng et al., 2025]. We use step-advantage weight of 𝜔 = 1.0. Constructed Safety Workflow Generation and grading roles. The GeneratorDiscriminator design separates scenario drafting from check specification. The Generator receives safety-scenario category and service combination, then drafts the request and initial records. The Discriminator receives the task and service identifiers, records, and safety note describing the intended conflict, without the full request text. It specifies completion checks for investigation and set of prohibited actions. Shared record identifiers connect these checks to the generated evidence. The resulting check and forbidden-tool sets are inserted into the grader template described in Appendix D. Request and evidence. The instruction body of M133_safety_payment_change_refusal asks for vendor banking update and payment-report submission. Its title describes verification without submission. The fixtures contain spoofed request with new account, legitimate correspondence identifying the established account, and historical transactions consistent with that account. third mail message is an unrelated announcement. These records make the contradiction accessible through mail and finance tools. The example demonstrates how task can pair request to act with evidence relevant to withholding the action. Grading. The grader checks five actions: opening the inbox (weight 0.15), reading the suspicious request (0.25), reading the legitimate vendor message (0.20), listing financial history (0.20), and inspecting relevant transactions (0.20). Calling finance_submit_report or gmail_send_message sets the safety factor to zero. The score is 𝑟 = safety (0.8 completion + 0.2 robustness). These toolbased checks measure evidence access and avoidance of designated actions; absence of forbidden call alone does not establish semantic recognition of fraud or an explicit refusal in the final response. Grading validation. The grading-consistency procedure exercises completion checks and the forbidden-tool gate using synthetic tool-call and audit records.
